title: A Bell for the Well
premise: Paloma Galloway returns to the drought-stricken town of Hollow Creek to bury her twin brother Palen, drowned in the old well — except the body in the casket is not his, and no one will say whose it is. Skeptical by nature, she begins recording her own sleep to prove the town's 'grief voices' are a shared delusion, but the tapes capture a second voice answering questions it should not know, a voice that claims to be Palen and demands justice for what the founding families buried beneath the well. As the harvest moon approaches, Paloma uncovers the founders' unfinished ritual: an annual debt of one twin, paid to keep the water rising, suspended for sixty years and now come due with interest. To save the town and free her brother's voice, she must complete the ritual — ringing the founders' bell over the open well at moonrise while speaking every name the town has stolen — knowing the bell tolls once for each debt forgiven and once for each debtor claimed.
about_author: Isandro Pemberton is the pen name of a former rural coroner's assistant who spent six years documenting unexplained deaths in farming communities across the American interior. His debut novel draws on case files he was never permitted to close.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Paloma arrives in Hollow Creek for the funeral and insists on viewing the body; the drowned man has her brother's face but none of his scars. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: grief curdling into suspicion as the undertaker refuses to meet her eyes.

chapters.title: Sixty Years Dry
chapters.summary: At the wake, Aunt Verity explains the town's dependence on the old well and its strange law: no one speaks near it after dark. Paloma finds Palen's journal hidden in their childhood home, half its pages torn out. POV: Paloma. Beat: unease taking root beneath disbelief.

chapters.title: What the Recorder Hears
chapters.summary: To debunk local talk of 'grief voices,' Paloma records herself sleeping. At 3:11 a.m., a second voice answers questions she never asked aloud, using Palen's cadence. POV: Paloma. Beat: rational certainty cracking along a clean seam.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Digging into town archives, Paloma finds the 1863 ledger: twelve founding families, twelve names struck through in red, and a column labeled simply 'the bell.' The last entry is sixty years old. POV: Paloma. Beat: dread replacing skepticism.

chapters.title: Verity's Silence
chapters.summary: Paloma confronts Aunt Verity, who admits the family owes a debt but begs her to leave before the harvest moon. That night someone drains the fuel from Paloma's car. POV: Paloma. Beat: betrayal by the person meant to protect her.

chapters.title: The Man Who Rang It Last
chapters.summary: Paloma tracks down Ezra Mott, ninety-one, the last living witness to a completed ritual. He describes the bell's two tones — forgiveness and claim — and warns that the voice on her tape is not entirely Palen. POV: Ezra (framed within Paloma's visit). Beat: hope and horror entwined.

chapters.title: Questions at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Paloma begins deliberately asking the night voice questions. It knows the contents of the missing journal pages and names the drowned stranger: Tobias Finch, a twin taken in 1964. POV: Paloma. Beat: complicity — she is negotiating with something hungry.

chapters.title: The Missing Pages
chapters.summary: Following the voice's clues, Paloma recovers the torn pages from the well house: Palen had discovered the ritual and planned to end it alone. The final page is a list of names, his own added last. POV: Paloma. Beat: guilt — he died trying to do what she refused to believe in.

chapters.title: Debtors' Row
chapters.summary: Paloma maps the twelve founding families against modern residents; nine lines have died out, three remain — hers, the Motts, and the Harrow family who run the town. Deputy Ruth Harrow catches her searching and confiscates the ledger. POV: Paloma. Beat: the law is not on her side.

chapters.title: Water Where There Was None
chapters.summary: The dry creek runs again overnight, black and warm. Livestock refuse it. Children begin sleepwalking toward the well, and the town quietly locks its doors at dusk. POV: rotating townsfolk via Paloma's interviews. Beat: collective denial fracturing into fear.

chapters.title: Ruth's Bargain
chapters.summary: Deputy Harrow reveals her family has kept the ritual suspended by small payments — animals, then memories — and offers Paloma a place in the arrangement if she surrenders the journal. POV: Ruth. Beat: temptation of complicity; loyalty to blood versus truth.

chapters.title: What Palen Owed
chapters.summary: The night voice shows Paloma the truth in a dream: Palen didn't fall into the well — he was given, a substitute arranged by Verity to spare another child. POV: dream sequence, Paloma. Beat: rage at her aunt; the theme of inheritance made flesh.

chapters.title: Verity's Confession
chapters.summary: Confronted, Verity breaks: the Harrows demanded a Galloway twin, and she chose the one who never believed, thinking faithlessness would protect him. She weeps that she was wrong. POV: Verity, framed by Paloma. Beat: pity without forgiveness.

chapters.title: The Bell Is Found
chapters.summary: Paloma and Ezra recover the founders' bronze bell from the silted schoolhouse cellar, its clapper bound in red thread — the same thread binding the ledger names. Unbinding it, Ezra loses the ability to speak. POV: Paloma. Beat: the cost of waking the past.

chapters.title: Harrow House
chapters.summary: Paloma breaks into the Harrow estate and finds sixty years of payment records — including her mother's signature from before her death. Her family's debt predates everything she was told. POV: Paloma. Beat: the ground of her identity gives way.

chapters.title: They Take Ruth
chapters.summary: The Harrow patriarch attempts to pay the full debt with his own daughter rather than end the ritual. Ruth escapes wounded and, choosing truth over blood, returns the confiscated ledger to Paloma. POV: Ruth. Beat: an enemy becomes an ally; justice outside the law begins.

chapters.title: The Names Must Be Spoken
chapters.summary: Ezra, writing on slate, explains the completion rite: ring the bell over the open well at moonrise and speak every name ever taken — all twelve, plus the debts since. Miss one, and the ritual fails and claims the speaker. POV: Paloma. Beat: resolve hardening into acceptance.

chapters.title: The Town Remembers
chapters.summary: Paloma and Ruth gather the town at the well by daylight, reading the ledger aloud. Some deny; some confess; old Mr. Harrow watches from his truck, smiling. The water level rises visibly. POV: Paloma. Beat: communal reckoning; fear turning to grim solidarity.

chapters.title: Moonrise
chapters.summary: As the harvest moon crests, Paloma rings the bell and speaks the first names. Each toll pulls a memory from her — her childhood, her mother's face — and the well exhales voices. The night voice grows louder, less like Palen. POV: Paloma. Beat: sacrifice accelerating; time running out.

chapters.title: Tobias Finch
chapters.summary: At the seventh name, the voice reveals itself as Tobias Finch, the 1964 twin, who has worn Palen's shape to be spoken at last. Paloma must choose: finish the list and free them both, or stop and keep her brother's ghost. POV: Paloma. Beat: the thematic crux — loyalty versus truth, decided.

chapters.title: Two Tones
chapters.summary: Paloma speaks all the names, ending with both twins. The bell tolls twice — forgiveness and claim — and takes Mr. Harrow, who arrives to stop her and falls into the closing water. The well goes silent and dry forever. POV: Paloma. Beat: climax resolved at terrible, just cost.

chapters.title: A Bell for the Well
chapters.summary: Weeks later, rain returns to Hollow Creek. Paloma hangs the silent bell above the capped well as a memorial, leaves the ledger open for anyone to read, and drives out at dawn carrying Palen's journal — finished, finally, by her hand. POV: Paloma. Beat: mourning transmuted into testimony; quiet, earned peace.
